name: Don't You Four Cheddar 'Bout Me Burger - (Comes with four kinds of cheddar)

recipe.history:
Cheddar cheese traces its origins to the village of Cheddar in Somerset, England, where cheesemakers were already producing it as far back as the 12th century. The Cheddar Gorge caves in Somerset provided ideal conditions — cool, humid, and stable in temperature — for aging the cheese to the firm, sharp perfection that would come to define the style. The process of 'cheddaring,' in which cut curds are stacked and turned repeatedly to expel whey and develop a dense, crumbly texture, was a distinctly English innovation. For centuries, authentic Somerset cheddar was a prestige product, wheel-aged for years, developing complex, tangy, almost crystalline depth. It was this cheese — nutty, sharp, and deeply savory — that English settlers eventually carried across the Atlantic, planting the seed of what would become the most consumed cheese in the world.

When cheddar arrived in America, it adapted with extraordinary enthusiasm to its new home. By the 19th century, New York State had become the center of industrial cheddar production, and the term 'American cheddar' was already diverging from its English ancestor — milder, more elastic, processed for mass appeal. Then came the hamburger, that great democratic American food, and the pairing was inevitable. The mild, clean melt of young American cheddar complemented the fat and salt of a beef patty perfectly, and by the mid-20th century 'cheeseburger' had become nearly synonymous with a cheddar-topped patty. The cheese's fat content and melt point made it technically ideal: it softened without breaking, pooled into the crevices of the meat, and added a lactic richness that amplified the beef's own umami. From diners to drive-throughs, cheddar became the default — the assumed, the beloved, the unremarkable standard against which all other burger cheeses are measured.

I remember the first time I truly understood that cheddar could be plural. I was at a small restaurant — the kind with mismatched chairs and a chalkboard menu — and the cook brought out a burger draped in what looked like a stained-glass window of melted cheese: pale yellow, deep orange, ivory white, and amber all running together at the edges. I took a bite and tasted something I hadn't expected: argument. The sharp bite of aged cheddar fighting with the buttery softness of a mild white, a smoked variety lending something almost campfire-like, and a raw-milk farmhouse cheddar tying it all together with grassy, earthy depth. It wasn't just a burger anymore — it was a conversation. I ate it at a wobbly table by a rain-streaked window, and I thought about how much a single ingredient can contain multitudes when you stop treating it as a monolith and start treating it as a family.

A burger cooked to medium rare — an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is not a preference. It is the correct answer to a question the beef is asking. At medium rare, the myoglobin in the muscle fibers remains intact and rosy, the intramuscular fat has rendered just enough to baste the meat from the inside, and the texture retains a yielding, almost tender resistance that well-done meat simply cannot offer. Cooking a burger past this point is an act of subtraction: you are driving off moisture, tightening proteins, and converting a living, complex thing into something dry and uniform. The crust — developed through high heat and the Maillard reaction — should contrast with a warm, pink, juicy interior, not encase a grey puck. This is not recklessness; it is respect. Use freshly ground beef from quality cuts, handle it minimally, and cook it to medium rare. Everything else is compromise.
ingredients: 300g bread flour, plus extra for dusting
3 large eggs, room temperature (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
680g (1.5 lbs) freshly ground beef — 80% lean chuck, 20% fat
1 tsp flaky sea salt (for seasoning exterior only)
1 tbsp neutral oil (canola or vegetable) for the pan or grill
4 slices sharp aged orange cheddar (2+ years aged, e.g., Tillamook Extra Sharp or Cabot Seriously Sharp)
4 slices mild white cheddar (young, creamy, e.g., Boar's Head Vermont White Cheddar)
4 slices smoked cheddar (cold-smoked, e.g., Beecher's Smoked Flagship or similar artisan smoked cheddar)
4 slices raw-milk farmhouse cheddar (e.g., Neal's Yard Clothbound or a local raw-milk aged cheddar)
Salt and black pepper to taste
1 large head green leaf lettuce, outer leaves removed, inner leaves separated and washed
1 large white or yellow onion, sliced into thin rings
8 slices dill pickle (bread-and-butter or kosher dill)
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — Combine warmed milk and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer; let bloom for 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, sugar, and salt. Mix on low with the dough hook until a shaggy dough forms, about 2 minutes.
2. Add 2 eggs one at a time, mixing on medium until each is fully incorporated. Increase speed to medium-high and knead for 5 minutes until the dough begins to come together.

3. With the mixer running on medium, add softened butter one cube at a time, waiting until each piece is absorbed before adding the next. This will take about 8 minutes. The dough should become smooth, glossy, and slightly tacky but not sticky.
4. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8–12 hours) for a cold ferment — this develops flavor and makes the dough easier to handle.

5. Remove dough from refrigerator and divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 155g each). Shape each into a tight round ball by cupping your hand over the dough on an unfloured surface and rolling in a tight circular motion. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing at least 3 inches apart.
6. Cover loosely with oiled plastic wrap and let proof at room temperature for 2–3 hours until noticeably puffed and pillowy.

7. Preheat oven to 190°C (375°F). Beat the remaining egg with 1 tsp water and brush gently over each bun. Sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool completely on a wire rack before slicing.

8. MAKE THE BURGER SAUCE — Whisk together mayonnaise, ketchup, yellow mustard, sweet relish, apple cider vinegar, garlic powder, onion powder, and smoked paprika in a small bowl. Season with salt and black pepper. Cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes to let flavors meld.

9. MAKE THE CHEDDAR SAUCE — Whisk cornstarch into cold milk in a small saucepan until dissolved. Add grated mild white cheddar, dry mustard, cayenne, and salt. Heat over medium-low, whisking constantly, until the sauce thickens and becomes smooth and pourable, about 4–5 minutes. Do not boil. Remove from heat, cover with a lid to keep warm, and whisk again just before serving.

10. FORM THE PATTIES — Remove ground beef from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking to take the chill off. Divide into 4 equal portions of approximately 170g (6 oz) each. Using minimal handling, gently form each into a disc about 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb — this prevents doming during cooking. Do NOT season until just before cooking.

11. PREPARE THE TOPPINGS — Slice tomatoes and lay on paper towels to drain excess moisture. Separate lettuce leaves. Slice onions into thin rings. Set pickles on a small plate. All toppings should be at room temperature.

12. COOK THE PATTIES — Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until it just begins to smoke. Add oil and swirl to coat. Season patties generously on both sides with flaky salt and cracked black pepper immediately before placing in the pan.
13. Cook patties over high heat for 2.5 minutes without moving, pressing gently once to ensure full contact with the surface. Flip once. Cook for a further 2 minutes on the second side.

14. APPLY THE FOUR CHEDDARS — Immediately after flipping, layer cheeses onto each patty in this order (bottom to top): one slice smoked cheddar, one slice aged sharp orange cheddar, one slice raw-milk farmhouse cheddar, one slice mild white cheddar. Add 1 tbsp of water to the edge of the pan and immediately cover with a lid or bowl for 45–60 seconds to create steam and melt all four layers simultaneously.

15. CHECK INTERNAL TEMPERATURE — Use an instant-read thermometer inserted into the side of the patty to confirm an internal temperature of 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Remove patties from heat and rest on a wire rack for 2 minutes — carryover cooking will bring temperature to approximately 135°F. Do not cook beyond this point.

16. TOAST THE BUNS — While patties rest, melt 2 tbsp butter on the skillet or in a separate pan over medium heat. Place buns cut-side down and toast until golden and lightly crisped, 1–2 minutes. Watch carefully.

17. ASSEMBLE THE BURGERS — Spread a generous layer of burger sauce on both the top and bottom bun cut faces. On the bottom bun, layer: 1–2 leaves of green leaf lettuce, 2 slices of tomato, a few onion rings, and 2 pickle slices.
18. Place the four-cheddar-draped patty directly on top of the pickles. Drizzle approximately 2 tbsp of warm cheddar sauce over the melted cheese stack, letting it run down the sides.
19. Cap with the top bun. Serve immediately — the window between perfect melt and cooling is brief, and this burger deserves to be eaten at its peak.
